props.title: The Believer

sections.content: The Believer stands as one of the most controversial and challenging films of the early 2000s. Ryan Gosling delivers a breakthrough performance as Danny Balint, a Jewish man who becomes a neo-Nazi - a premise based on the true story of Daniel Burros. The film shares thematic DNA with American History X (1998) but pushes even further into uncomfortable territory by exploring the psychological complexity of self-hatred. Director Henry Bean crafts scenes of brutal violence alongside intimate moments of religious contemplation, creating a disorienting portrait that echoes the protagonist's internal conflict.

sections.content: The film's exploration of faith and identity connects it to other provocative works about religious conflict like Paradise Now (2005) and Jesus Camp (2006). But Bean's approach is uniquely philosophical, incorporating actual Talmudic debates into heated arguments between characters. The movie's unflinching examination of antisemitism from within the Jewish community itself makes it particularly controversial, yet it's this very complexity that elevates it beyond simple moral messaging.

Gosling's portrayal laid groundwork for other actors tackling similarly complex roles about ideological extremism, like Daniel Radcliffe in Imperium (2016) and Edward Norton in American History X (1998). The film's influence can be seen in later works like Skin (2018), which also deals with the transformation of identity within hate movements. SUBHEAD: Religious Identity and Extremism in Cinema

sections.content: The Believer arrived at a crucial moment when films began more directly confronting religious extremism and identity. Works like Paradise Now (2005) and United 93 (2006) would soon follow, examining radicalization from different angles. Bean's film stands apart by focusing on the psychological rather than political aspects of extremism, making it more aligned with character studies like Taxi Driver (1976) than with issue-driven documentaries.
